I constantly see people reviewing books or series as a "high fantasy" or "epic fantasy", I know fantasy is pretty broad, but what does each subgenre mean, in layman's terms?
What do all the different types of fantasy mean? (ie - Epic Fantasy, High Fantasy, etc.)

It all depends on how the little man behaves. If he sings folk songs for kings and saves the world, it's high fantasy. But if he chases prostitutes and shoots his dad with a crossbow while he's trying to go to the bathroom, it's low fantasy.

Generally high fantasy is anything with elves and dragons and the like in a medieval setting or one radically different from the contemporary world. Low fantasy are those with similar elements to high fantasy, but in a contemporary setting. So something like Dungeons and Dragons is high fantasy while Vampire the Masquerade is low fantasy.

High fantasy is a drastically different world from our own. The rules of reality may be completely different, and there's usually a shit ton of fantasy races.

Epic fantasy is fantasy that is epic in scope. Stuff like Tolkien, which chronicles every part of the history of the entire world (from its creation through the end of the third age) definitely falls into this realm. Smaller scale stuff like the first two thirds of The Hobbit wouldn't fall into this category since its much smaller in scale. The last bits of the book get into the War of Five Armies though, which gets much more epic in scale!

Low fantasy is more along the lines of "our world with a bit of a push", or by "exposing" elements of the world that the general public is unaware of. A good example might be Harry Potter, which supposedly takes place in our world and reality but shows us a hidden side of it.

So here are a few definitions and examples:

(Examples are neither definitive or the top works in the field, they are just the one's I've read and came to mind as I typed away...)

Comic fantasy is mostly humorous, generally fixating on parody or absurd situations - John Dechancie's Castle Perilous series is an example, as is Robert Asprin's MythAdventures

Contemporary fantasy is set in a recognizable 'real' world but includes magic or other supernatural elements - Mary Poppins, Harry Potter, The Percy Jackson series and about half of Mercedes Lackey's work fall into this category.

Urban Fantasy is a growing sub-genre of Contemporary, almost a genre in it's own respect at this point, it is Contemporary Fantasy, but almost exclusively set in a city. Jim Butcher's The Dresden Files is a fine example of this type (and a personal favorite)

Dark fantasy features horror - HP Lovecraft and Clive Barker - 'nuff said.

High fantasy or epic fantasy generally has a plot and/or themes that are epic in scale. Or put more succinctly, focus on the nobility and the fate of nations and generally also include overt fantastic elements and creatures - elves, dragons, functional magic, etc. Lord of the Rings and Tad Williams' Memory, sorrow, and Thorn fit here.

Low fantasy is either fantasy with few supernatural elements or one that focuses on those of "common" birth.Game Of Thrones fits here, more or less, for having many character of "common" station, and few traditional fantasy elements.

Romantic fantasy is any harlequin romance that includes supernatural elements. Odd enough, Dracula fits here in addition to being a Gothic Fantasy story.

Gothic Fantasy is Fantasy with a 'Dark Edge' but not usually outright horror. Gormenghast is a prime example.

Science fantasy mixes fantasy and science fiction. the game ShadowRun and the 80s cartoons Thundarr the Barbarian and ThunderCats go here.

Sword and sandal, adventures of low characters making their way by the might of their sword. Conan the Cimmerian is the usual master of this genre.

(Edits: fixed italics and overall readability)
Excellent summary of the genre. I've always been confused by this. Does contemporary fantasy essentially translate to hard scifi?

For certain values of "sci-fi" I would think it does. Not "hard sci-fi" as such, as hard sci-fi is usually applied to stories that remain well within the current understanding of the laws of physics. The Mars Series by Kim Stanley Robinson, most everything by Michael Crichton (Jurassic Park, etc.) or The first three-quarters of 2001 are "Hard Sci-Fi".

"Soft sci-fi" is that which includes advanced technologies that are often functionally indistinguishable from magic (props to Professor Clarke). Doc Smith's Lensman or Dune are good examples. Any soft sci-fi set in a modern day 'real-world' setting would be hard to fully separate from Contemporary Fantasy. Charles Stross's The Jennifer Morgue leaps to mind, as it takes both Contemporary Fantasy, and soft sci-fi, dumps them in a blender and hits 'frappe'.

You are absolutely right! I was on the fence about using GoT as an example. GoT starts as low fantasy, focusing on a world with few elements of magic. The first book has few instances of anything resembling magic. The Wights of the Others and the birth of the dragons are the only really 'magical' occurrences. Dire Wolves are not precisely magic, being a real but extinct species from the pleistocene era. Dragons were rumor and legends, and even when finally born (which was magical) are treated as critters with a unusual biology, rather than inherently magical beasts. There are swords of unusual steel, but, again not magical. In later books, the magic of the dragons become more obvious, from their fantastic grown rate to their flight and fire. Spells that work, such as the fire and water resurrection spells appear, as well as the Red Priestess's magical protections. Other "fantasy" races come into play, such as giants and the elfin children of the forest. So, Game of Thrones is a series that started as a low fantasy and is building progressively to a high fantasy. Conan can certainly be considered low fantasy. But can also be considered epic, due to the sweep of empires that Conan interacts with, and can be alternate history, as Hyborea is a version of Europe and Africa before a great flood, and can be science fantasy for the reason you pointed out. As with almost all great and seminal works, pinning them down to a single genre is usually difficult, so I made generalizations. I guess these should be considered guidelines, at best. The best way to really define genre is to read for yourself and file the works mentally in the way that works best for you.

Something to consider about streaming. If they can successfully stream the video frame rate and quality to a device AND have the controls be responsive enough, they will start do this with AAA games in the future. I am currently working on projects that do full 3D rendering with user interactions across large distances with little to no noticeable lag. Once they have the ability to scale this and have it at a cost effective price point, the consoles will just become dumb devices. This means all games can be developed for hardware running in Sony's, Nintendo's, or Microsoft's data center and consoles are just a controller and video output. Never needing to be updated until the next version of controllers, USB, or video output e.g. HDMI.

If your math skills are terrible, you will find programming exceedingly difficult. Programming IS math. Although in everyday programming you wont use super complex formulas, the way you approach design and problem solving involves core principles of mathematics. Order of operations, solving problems in steps, relations and the ideas of the x,y vertex are the basics. As you move down to lower level programming or you wish to move into more complex applications you'll need further understanding of it. Graphics will have you deal in screen areas, video games will have you calculating all sorts of things. But all of it boils down to firm grasp of logic.

However if you really want to get better at something what you really need is the passion for it. If you find some joy in it then I suggest starting in C. It doesn't deal with Object oriented programing like java, C++ or C# it will help you start to learn the logic of programming and when you move to a higher level language of programming you'll have a firmer understanding of whats happening.

So, I'm shit at math. I've always been shit at math and I have about the concentration span of a fly. One day, I realized that I had wanted to become a programmer my whole life (little 6 year old vaporwaif was very inspired by Java on the Brain and wanted to grow up to make cool free games with penguins and robots, too) and had defeated myself out of a dream so effectively that I didn't even realize I could try. So, I tried - I signed up for a couple intro to Java classes and my college's absolute easiest math class that still satisfies GE where I realized two things: * Math isn't that hard if you don't worry too much about the significance of each formula and just follow their instructions instead - once you get into a groove of it, it's fun. *Programming, for whatever reason, can keep the attention span of a fly. I was working on an assignment for 9 hours straight. I did not take breaks because I didn't think about it. (Clearly, I love taking breaks - I'm on Voat right now!) I was having fun solving the puzzle of doing the things I wanted to do.   The moral of the story is that even if you're going to be slow at something, it will be fine if you think it's interesting and if you can slow yourself down. I realize that doesn't sound like it makes sense because it sounds like just being extra slow, but you will accomplish what you want to accomplish very effectively if you just focus on the task at hand. So now I'm studying Computer Engineering because fuck it, why not? I failed my Summer trig class (grades 90% testing, 10% homework, old-school Russian grading on tests) but I'm not even that bummed about it because I kept on top of it the whole time so now I feel like I'm going to go kill it in the fall. Better tl;dr moral: If you want to do a thing, don't trip. Do the thing.

It's not so much about being good at math, so much as, "do you like math?". Or more specifically, "do you like solving problems which have an element of mathematics in them?"

You don't need to be a genius at math to solve a sudoku puzzle. But you do have to like math to start to understand the algorithm behind the solution.

You get good at math by practice, so yeah you start out terrible and become better as you solve problems.

I recommend starting out with some easy Project Euler problems and working your way up to more difficult problems as you get better.
